question: A learner claims: 'decomposeSO reconstructs ANY orthogonal matrix A (A.transpose*A=1) as a product of adjacent RY planes, because planeMatrix is orthogonal and the sweep zeroes out the subdiagonal.' Identify the missing hypothesis, give a 2x2 counterexample, and explain precisely where the reconstruction proof would fail without it.
reference_answer: The missing hypothesis is det A = 1 (special orthogonal). decomposeSO_action requires BOTH orthogonal (A.transpose*A=1) AND determinant (A.det=1). Each planeMatrix has determinant exactly 1 (planeMatrix_det), so any product of them -- hence stepsMatrix(decomposeSO A) -- also has determinant 1. Therefore a reflection with det = -1 can never be written as such a product. Counterexample: A = [[1,0],[0,-1]] (a reflection) satisfies A.transpose*A = 1 but det A = -1. Running the sweep: columnSweep already fixes the first column to e_0 (it is), and the residual after the full prefix is the diagonal matrix diag(1,-1). The step that fails is `matrix_eq_one_of_last_prefix`: it uses det A = 1 to force the final diagonal entry A_last,last = +1 (via det of the diagonal = product of diagonal entries = 1). With det = -1 the last entry is -1, the residual is diag(1,-1) != 1, so fullSweep does NOT reach the identity and the reconstruction identity decomposeSO_action breaks. In short: orthogonality alone gives |A_last,last| = 1 (orthogonal_supported_column_sq gives the square is 1) but only det=1 selects the +1 branch; adjacent RY planes generate SO(N), not all of O(N).

question: Let H = C^d with the standard inner product of Eq. (2.4), and let |psi> in H be a unit vector, <psi|psi> = 1. Define rho := |psi><psi|. Starting only from Definition 2.1 (a quantum state is a density operator with rho >= 0 and tr rho = 1), prove that rho is a legitimate quantum state, that it is a rank-one orthogonal projector (rho^2 = rho = rho^dagger), and explain in what precise sense this makes rho an extreme point (pure state) of the convex set of density operators. State explicitly which step uses normalization of |psi> and why dropping it breaks the trace condition.
reference_answer: Hermiticity: rho^dagger = (|psi><psi|)^dagger = |psi><psi| = rho. Positivity: for any |phi>, <phi|rho|phi> = <phi|psi><psi|phi> = |<psi|phi>|^2 >= 0, hence rho >= 0. Trace/normalization: in any orthonormal basis, tr rho = sum_i <e_i|psi><psi|e_i> = <psi|(sum_i |e_i><e_i|)|psi> = <psi|psi> = 1, where the final equality is exactly the unit-norm hypothesis computed with the Eq. (2.4) inner product. Both Definition 2.1 conditions hold, so rho is a quantum state. Idempotency: rho^2 = |psi><psi|psi><psi| = <psi|psi>|psi><psi| = rho, so rho is an orthogonal projector onto the one-dimensional span{|psi>}, hence rank 1. Extreme point: if rho = p sigma_1 + (1-p) sigma_2 with 0<p<1 and density operators sigma_i, positivity forces the range of each sigma_i inside range(rho) = span{|psi>}; the only trace-one state supported on a one-dimensional space is |psi><psi|, so sigma_1 = sigma_2 = rho and the decomposition is trivial. Thus rho is an extreme point (pure state), matching the text's statement that a pure density matrix has rank 1 and equals a projector |psi><psi|. If normalization were dropped (<psi|psi> = c != 1) then tr rho = c != 1 violates Definition 2.1, and (|psi><psi|)^2 = c|psi><psi| != rho, so one must renormalize rho = |psi><psi|/<psi|psi> to recover a state.

question: Consider the two-qubit EPR/Bell state |Phi+>_AB = (1/sqrt 2)(|0>_A|0>_B + |1>_A|1>_B) with density matrix Phi+_AB = |Phi+><Phi+| as in Eqs. (2.17)-(2.18). Using the defining relation Eq. (2.14), tr(rho_AB (X_A tensor 1_B)) = tr(rho_A X_A) for all X_A, and/or the basis formula Eq. (2.15), compute the marginal rho_A = tr_B Phi+_AB and show rho_A = (1/2) 1 (Eq. (2.22)). Explain why this maximally mixed marginal shows Phi+ is not a product state, and why the partial trace is independent of the orthonormal basis chosen in Eq. (2.15).
reference_answer: Write |Phi+> = (1/sqrt2) sum_{i in {0,1}} |i>_A|i>_B. Using Eq. (2.15) with the computational B-basis: tr_B Phi+_AB = sum_k (1_A tensor <k|_B) |Phi+><Phi+| (1_A tensor |k>_B). Since (1_A tensor <k|_B)|Phi+> = (1/sqrt2)|k>_A, each term is (1/2)|k>_A<k|_A, and summing over k in {0,1} gives rho_A = (1/2)(|0><0| + |1><1|) = (1/2)1, the maximally mixed state (Eq. 2.22). Equivalently via Eq. (2.14): tr(Phi+_AB (X_A tensor 1_B)) = (1/2)(<0|X_A|0> + <1|X_A|1>) = (1/2) tr X_A = tr((1/2)1 X_A) for all X_A, so by uniqueness rho_A = (1/2)1. Not a product state: a pure global state has a pure marginal iff it is a product; here rho_A = (1/2)1 is maximally mixed (eigenvalues 1/2,1/2, rank 2), so if Phi+ = omega_A tensor sigma_B its A-marginal would be the pure omega_A, contradicting rho_A = (1/2)1. A pure global state with a mixed marginal is by definition entangled. Basis independence: Eq. (2.14) defines rho_A uniquely by its action against all X_A with no reference to a basis; Eq. (2.15) merely evaluates that unique operator, so every orthonormal {|e_i>_B} yields the same rho_A, as the text explicitly notes.
